newsitem.title: USA: Americans may have to consider driving less - panel.
newsitem.headline: Americans may have to consider driving less - panel.

text.p: The United States may soon need to consider policies to discourage driving and develop cars that use cleaner fuels or less oil to help stem global warming, a National Research Council panel said Thursday.

However, the panel said the government will first have to educate the public intensively about the risks of climate change and the effects of pollution from cars and trucks if it decides to pursue policies such as raising fuel taxes.

The group focused on cars and trucks in the United States because they account for 5 percent of the world's entire carbon dioxide emissions, which scientists believe are a major contributor to global warming.

"Though this percentage appears modest, no other energy use sector in the United States or elsewhere in the world accounts for a significantly larger portion of global CO2 emissions," the panel of environment, economics, transportation and public policy experts said in a report.

U.S. pollution would be even worse if the mid-1970s oil crisis had not pushed Americans into driving smaller cars, said James Hebert, a marine biology professor at Johns Hopkins University and chairman of the panel.

"But we've allowed ourselves to get soft and adopt measures that we know deep within the recesses of our minds are not wise," he said in a telephone interview, pointing to the skyrocketing demand for sport utility vehicles.

The report comes as the Clinton administration puts together its position for international talks on a climate change treaty, to be signed in December, to make industrialized countries trim their carbon emissions.

The administration has all but ruled out a carbon tax as a way to discourage oil, gas and coal use, the main source of carbon emissions, having run into fierce opposition to higher energy taxes four years ago.
If car and fuel use follows today's trends, annual carbon emissions from U.S. motor vehicles could more than double within the next 50 years, the report said.
The panel called for more research into the factors that influence travel demand, and more research into alternative transportation technology, fuels, and the impact of pollution.
